qs.q: In the HELPERR algorithm, which step directly follows "Enter vagina" (internal rotation)?
o: Roll the patient onto all fours
Apply suprapubic pressure to the abdomen
Hyperflex the thighs using the McRoberts maneuver
Remove the posterior arm from the fetal shoulder
qs.e: After internal rotation, the next recommended maneuver is removal of the posterior arm. The other steps occur earlier or later in the sequence.

qs.q: A 19-year-old woman is diagnosed with clear cell adenocarcinoma of the upper anterior vagina. This rare malignancy is most strongly associated with which of the following prenatal exposures?
qs.e: Clear cell adenocarcinoma of the vagina is strongly linked to in utero exposure to diethylstilbestrol (DES). It develops in young women whose mothers took DES, leading to vaginal adenosis.
qs.s: Disorders of the Vagina and Breast: MCQs

qs.q: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the clinic with soft, grape-like polypoid masses protruding from the vagina and associated vaginal bleeding. Biopsy shows a cambium layer. What is the diagnosis?
qs.e: Sarcoma botryoides (embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma) is the most common malignant vaginal tumor in infants and young girls under 5 years, presenting as soft grape-like masses. It features a characteristic cambium layer of dense subepithelial tumor cells.

qs.q: Clear cell adenocarcinoma of the vagina in young women is most strongly associated with
o: Germline BRCA1 mutations in affected patients
qs.e: Clear cell adenocarcinoma of the vagina develops in young women whose mothers took DES during pregnancy. DES causes vaginal adenosis, which is the precursor lesion.

qs.q: An XX chromosome baby is born with a penis, scrotum with no testes, no vagina. Which could cause this? ---
o: Abnormally high levels of circulating testosterone in the maternal blood
Abnormally high levels of human chorionic gonadotropin by trophoblast cells
Abnormally high levels of luteinizing hormone in the maternal blood
Abnormally low rates of estrogen production by the developing placenta
qs.e: Ejaculation requires coordinated autonomic and somatic motor pathways. Damage to lower spinal motor neurons can disrupt the somatic component and prevent normal ejaculation.

es.q: A 4-year-old girl presents with a rapidly growing, grape-like mass protruding from her vagina. Biopsy shows small primitive cells with a characteristic subepithelial condensation of tumor cells. What is the most likely diagnosis? → Sarcoma botryoides (Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma)
es.m:
**Diagnosis**
- Sarcoma botryoides
- Also known as embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma
- Most common malignant vaginal tumor in children under 5 years

**Clinical Presentation**
- Rapidly growing, grape-like (botryoid) mass
- Protrudes from the vaginal introitus
- May cause vaginal bleeding or discharge

**Histology**
- Small, primitive round cells
- Subepithelial condensation of tumor cells (cambium layer)
- Positive for desmin and myogenin (muscle markers)

ai.title: Vaginal Pathology
ai.subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
ai.summary: Vaginal disease ranges from common infections to serious pelvic inflammatory disease. Clinicians must recognise red flags, use limited investigations, and treat the underlying cause while monitoring for complications.

sections.p: Vaginal pathology refers to any abnormality of the vaginal mucosa, lumen or surrounding tissues. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by simple tests when available.

t.b: Detects Gram‑positive cocci or Gram‑negative diplococci – indicates bacterial vaginosis or gonorrhoea; a positive result directs specific antibiotics.
Identifies clue cells (Gardnerella) or yeast hyphae; guides treatment of bacterial vaginosis or candidiasis.

sections.p: Severity is graded by extent of inflammation and systemic signs. Simple staging: mild (localized), moderate (pelvic pain, fever), severe (sepsis, tubo‑ovarian abscess).
In low‑resource settings, infections dominate. Common first‑line causes are listed by category.

t.b: Screen for HIV to guide STI management and anticipate immune status.
Detects syphilis; a positive result changes antibiotic choice and informs partner treatment.

sections.p: Symptoms vary with cause but often include abnormal discharge, odour, itching, pain, bleeding, or fever.
Limited tests are useful; when unavailable, clinical judgment prevails.

faq.q: What is the first antibiotic choice for PID in a low‑resource setting?
faq.a: Doxycycline plus metronidazole covers gonorrhoea, chlamydia and anaerobes; it is affordable and effective.

faq.q: How do you differentiate bacterial vaginosis from candidiasis?
faq.a: BV has a fishy odour, greenish discharge, and clue cells on microscopy; candidiasis has white curd‑like discharge, itching, and hyphae on wet mount.
When ultrasound shows a tubo‑ovarian abscess >3 cm or the patient is deteriorating despite antibiotics.

exam: What is the most likely diagnosis in a woman with fishy discharge and a positive Gram stain for Gram‑negative diplococci? — Gonorrhoea; treat with ceftriaxone and partner notification.

A patient presents with foul discharge, pelvic pain, and fever. What is the next best step? — Perform a pelvic ultrasound to look for an abscess; if unavailable, start empirical doxycycline + metronidazole.
Why is metronidazole avoided in pregnancy? — It is teratogenic; use clindamycin instead.
Which sign distinguishes bacterial vaginosis from candidiasis? — Fishy odour and green discharge vs. white curd‑like discharge and itching.
What red flag would prompt immediate referral for a woman with vaginal discharge? — Rapidly increasing abdominal pain and fever >38.5°C.
How do you manage a patient with suspected PID but no access to ultrasound? — Start empirical antibiotics and monitor vitals; if no improvement in 48–72h, refer for drainage.
